title: Is it common now to use AI for almost all the game development?
author: Able_Tell9927
selftext:
I worked as a backend developer before, and now I am a product manager.    
I always wanted to make my own game, but before AI, making a game alone was really painful and frustrating for me. There are too many things need to learn and handle, like coding, framework, bugs, UI, art and game design.    
Now AI agents are getting much stronger. I feel like I finally have a chance to make a game by myself, but work a little bit like a small team.    
I just started my first indie game. It is a factory simulator, and now I am still working on the basic prototype.    
So I want to ask, is it common now for indie developers to use AI during almost the whole development process?    
And for me, as a person with ADHD, this way also helps me keep moving and not give up so easily.

replies.author: Jolly-Rip5973
replies.body:
How it will EVENTUALLY go down; 

1) you use human concepts artist to create concept artwork.   
2) you train an Ai model on the concept art.   
3) you use ai tools to generate assets.   
4) each asset is reviewed, rejected, accepted, or tagged for correction.   
5) a human artists using traditional manual tools make any necessary corrections or embellishments.   
6) Each goes through workflow using different AI models or different manual tools .   
7) Art director keep tight control over the whole thing to maintain the artistic vision and coherence.   
  
Large studios will have two new departments.   
Department for dataset acquisition, development and collation.   
Department for training and fine tuning in house AI models.   
  
 Most AI models used will only do one specific step in workflow with human judgement, quality control and correction at each steps. For example;  
  
One model takes a sketch and creates 3D model from it.   
which a human artist cleans up.   
  
Another model creates a skin.     
which a human artist cleans up.  
  
Another model takes 3D model and add animation bones.  
which a human artist cleans up.   
  
Another model add animation to the model with bones.   
which a human cleans up.   
  
this part gets iterated over and over to cover all needed animations.   
Animations will mostly be done with reference videos, you basically don't need a full mocap system any longer. There are models that can create animations for any reference video.

There are a couple of projects I've seen in this space that are using it for art more specifically with interesting purposes but otherwise it's mostly to speed up code.

replies.author: arscene

Things that have already been done and can be found as package or add-ons, we buy them. It's nice to have pieces that do the heavy lifting without having to maintain them yourself.

Other than that we already have workflows.

replies.author: SnuffleBag
replies.body:
>Its easy to make a game fully with AI.

It really isn't. This is why there currently exists exactly 0 good and/or commercially successful games fully made with AI.

It's easy to make something that gives the impression of being the promising beginnings of a game, and then lean on a crutch of "this was soo easy to make, imagine the potential" while never actually realizing said potential. Don't get fooled into thinking you can "just have AI make the game with a little human direction", AI is nowhere near at this level yet.

replies.author: fued
replies.body:
Its easy to make a game.
Its hard to make a good game.

That was my entire point.

replies.author: SnuffleBag
replies.body:
By that reasoning you could claim that creating a new template starter project is 'making a game', in which case it's also easy to make a game without AI ;)

It's not just about being a 'good game', but about being a high-quality production to expected industry standards. If AI could make a boring game with highly polished, coherent visuals, a perfectly balanced soundscape, great looking animations, responsive controls etc that would be one thing.. but it can't - all these sensationalist posts look like someone's first tutorial project, with the core focus being on how easy it was to make, not on how any part of it actually stands up to even the most basic scrutiny.

comments.author: geddy
comments.body:
I’m a software engineer, but I never dabbled in game development. Too much insane math that just isn’t what I find fun to work on.

I’ve always had ideas floating around in my head of interesting games that I would like to play, so I’ve used it quite a bit to put some smaller games together. Think multiplayer browser games, not fully fledged action adventure experiences. It’s been great for doing that sort of stuff, but I still spend several days making tweaks to the code, cleaning it up, that sort of thing. 

Anyway, the reason I bring this up is because I can’t imagine that actual game developers, engineers who KNOW how to do all of this, aren’t using these tools to speed up the process. 

I specialize more in web development, I use it but to a lesser extent because I understand it front to back. And when I do use it, my prompts are extremely detailed because I know what I want - this is how I assume game developers use it. However, if they needed a website to advertise their game, I imagine they might use these tools the way I do, “just get me something running” because they focus their effort on the games.

I thought about this a lot lately and that’s what I landed on. Would love to hear some insight from other software engineers.

replies.author: Able_Tell9927
replies.body:
Yes, I think the most important thing is that you clearly understand how your workflow works. Every time you ask AI to do something, you should know what it is doing and understand why it is doing it. That is how you can make sure the project is still maintainable.  
I don’t think every version needs to be perfect. The more important thing is that you can keep iterating on the system. You also need to think about future features early enough, so the structure can support them later. Otherwise, when you want to add a new feature, you may suddenly find that there is no data structure or system underneath to support it.  
So based on this idea, I think AI can help us handle some of the boring and repetitive work, while humans become more like the managers and decision makers.

That’s especially true for me since I have ADHD. Getting fast, visible feedback makes it much easier for me to stay engaged.

replies.author: Able_Tell9927
replies.body:
Yeah. When I work on version 2.0, I usually add the new features and changes under the 1.0 design document first. Then I let the AI merge everything into a complete 2.0 document and also summarize what changed from the previous version.  
That’s how I’m doing it for now.

replies.author: Able_Tell9927
replies.body:
My current workflow is roughly like this:  
I first use ChatGPT conversations to work through the requirements in detail. Then I decide what should go into the current version based on priority. At this stage, most of my updates are actually laying the groundwork for future features — things like basic pathfinding, a building system, save/load, and so on.  
Once the scope is clear, I let GPT-6 Astra review the current codebase and turn the requirements into an implementation plan, usually broken down into phases like P0–P6.  
Then I use GPT-6 Sol as the main agent, with Luna working as a sub-agent to implement the features. Sol is responsible for reviewing the work and checking the overall quality and architecture.  
Finally, I run the test cases, playtest the game myself, and fix the smaller issues and details that come up.  
If anyone is interested, I’ll keep sharing my development progress and workflow as the project moves forward. I’d be happy to discuss it with everyone here.

comments.author: LAGameStudio

comments.author: Slapbox98

It definitely isn't one prompt and a game appears, though. I still have to decide what I want, break it into small pieces, test each change in the browser and catch when the result doesn't match what I had in mind. The best part for me is being able to try an idea quickly. The hard part is keeping all the changes working together.
